issues.legal_issue: A second appeal permits interference with factual findings only when it involves a substantial question of law and the requirements for that question are satisfied.
material_facts: The High Court allowed a second appeal seeking recovery of possession after framing questions based on the supposed inconsistency between refusal of possession and an award of mesne profits, and on the declaration of title to half the property.
The First Appellate Court had examined the evidence and title documents and reached reasoned findings about the parties’ respective ownership.
The High Court’s questions did not raise a debatable legal issue, an error in construing a document, a violation of settled law, or a recognized basis for disturbing the factual findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not use second-appeal jurisdiction to reanalyse or disturb the First Appellate Court’s findings; the questions it framed were not substantial questions of law, and its decision allowing the second appeal was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal lies only if the case involves a substantial question of law, which must be formulated and decided as required by that section. A question must be debatable or involve a material violation of settled law, have a foundation in the pleadings and sustainable factual findings, and be necessary to decide the case. A mere question of fact or application of settled principles to facts is insufficient. Factual findings are generally not open to challenge, subject to recognized exceptions such as ignored material evidence, no evidence, erroneous legal inferences, or an incorrectly placed burden of proof. The Court relied on Sir Chunilal v. Mehta & Sons Ltd., Hero Vinoth v. Seshammal, Panchagopal Barua v. Vinesh Chandra Goswami, Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, Ramchandra v. Ramalingam, Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar, and Biswanath Ghosh v. Gobinda Ghose.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from an appellate decree to a higher court.
predicates.no_substantial_question_of_law: The appeal raises no debatable legal issue with a material bearing on the decision and no material departure from settled law.

issues.definition: When an appeal from an appellate decree raises no substantial legal issue, the higher court cannot use it to reopen factual findings.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration of title does not by itself entitle a claimant to recovery of possession from an actual possessor; the claimant must establish entitlement to possession and that the claim is not barred by limitation.
material_facts: The First Appellate Court found that the plaintiff owned one portion of the property and the defendant owned another, but the defendant was in possession of the whole property.
The defendant asserted in the written statement that he had possessed and occupied the property as owner for years, including continuous possession from the time of a release deed.
The plaintiff did not state in the plaint when the defendant or his predecessor took possession or facts showing that the claim for possession was within limitation.
The plaintiff did not establish the alleged landlord-and-tenant relationship, and the First Appellate Court had refused recovery of possession.
The High Court granted possession based on the defendant’s failure to plead adverse possession expressly.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in granting possession. The First Appellate Court’s refusal of that relief was restored, while its declaration of the plaintiff’s title to a portion of the property remained in place.
issues.legal_principle: A decree for possession does not automatically follow a declaration of title. The claimant must establish entitlement to possession and that the claim is not barred by limitation; the Court also stated that a claimant must show possession before the alleged trespasser took possession. Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires dismissal of a time-barred suit even if limitation is not pleaded in defence, and Articles 64 and 65 prescribe limitation rules for possession claims based respectively on prior possession and title. The presumption that possession follows title applies only where the property’s nature does not admit actual and exclusive occupation and there is no definite proof of another person’s possession. A claimant must succeed on the strength of the claimant’s own case, not the opponent’s weakness. The Court relied on Baba Kartar Singh v. Dayal Das and Peri v. Chrishold. It observed that the defendant’s pleaded claim of long possession as owner was, in substance, a defence of adverse possession, but did not decide whether the defendant had acquired title by adverse possession.

predicates.possession_suit: The claimant seeks recovery of possession of immovable property in a civil proceeding.
predicates.defendant_in_actual_possession: The opposing party is in actual possession of the property claimed.
predicates.plaintiff_fails_to_establish_entitlement: The claimant does not establish both a right to obtain possession and that the claim for possession is within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: In a civil suit for possession, an actual possessor cannot be ordered to surrender property when the claimant has not established both entitlement to possession and a timely claim.

issues.legal_issue: A refusal of possession is not inconsistent with an award of reimbursement for use or occupation unless the court has in fact awarded mesne profits based on wrongful possession.
material_facts: The First Appellate Court refused recovery of possession but held that the defendant was liable to make over any income derived from the plaintiff’s portion or pay charges for its use, occupation, or enjoyment.
The First Appellate Court did not use the term mesne profits and made no finding that the defendant’s possession was wrongful.
The High Court treated the First Appellate Court as having awarded mesne profits and considered that award inconsistent with refusing possession.
issues.conclusion: The High Court proceeded on an erroneous factual premise: the First Appellate Court had not awarded mesne profits, so the asserted inconsistency did not arise.
issues.legal_principle: Mesne profits are profits that a person in wrongful possession of property might have derived, excluding profits attributable to improvements. A direction concerning income or charges for use, occupation, or enjoyment is not, without more, an award of mesne profits. The Court applied this distinction in assessing whether the lower court’s rulings were inconsistent.

predicates.possession_refused: The court declines to order the opposing party to deliver possession to the claimant.
predicates.use_or_occupation_reimbursement_allowed: The court allows recovery of income or charges associated with use, occupation, or enjoyment of the claimant’s property.
predicates.no_finding_of_wrongful_possession: The court makes no finding that the opposing party possessed the property wrongfully.

issues.definition: A refusal of possession and an allowance of use-related reimbursement are not inconsistent as to mesne profits when wrongful possession has not been found.

issues.legal_issue: A pleading that claims continuous possession as owner of property beyond the claimant’s established ownership may amount in substance to a defence of adverse possession even without using that label.
material_facts: The defendant was found to own only a portion of the property but admitted possession of the entire property.
In the written statement, the defendant claimed continuous possession of the property as owner for years and asserted ownership under conveyance and release documents.
The defendant did not expressly plead adverse possession in those words.
issues.conclusion: In the circumstances, the defendant’s written statement was in substance a defence of adverse possession, although the Court did not decide whether the defendant was entitled to title on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The substance of a party’s pleaded claim, rather than the use of a particular label, may show that the party has advanced a defence of adverse possession. The Court expressly left open whether the defendant had established a right to title by adverse possession.

predicates.property_title_suit: The proceeding concerns a claim to ownership or possession of immovable property.
predicates.defendant_claims_continuous_possession_a: The defendant pleads continuous possession of the property in the character of owner.
predicates.defendant_claims_more_property_than_esta: The defendant’s claimed possession as owner extends beyond the portion of the property the defendant is found to own.

issues.definition: In a property title proceeding, a defendant’s claim of continuous ownership-like possession beyond the defendant’s established title amounts in substance to an adverse-possession defence.
